text.p: Nigeria's ruling generals met on Tuesday to finish work on a 1997 fiscal budget that they said would address the plight of ordinary people.

"Budget 1997 is going to be the budget for growth and development," said Major-General John Inienger, a member of the Provisional Ruling Council (PRC), who addressed reporters after their first session in the capital Abuja on Monday.
The day military ruler General Sani Abacha will announce the budget was expected to be set after Tuesday's meeting.
Normally budgets are broadcast on New Year's Day, but they have been delayed every year since 1993 when Abacha took power.
After two years of trying to stabilise key facets of Nigeria's economy, his government is widely expected to unveil a reflationary package in the 1997 budget to stimulate growth.

The World Bank and local economists have praised Abacha for rescuing an economy that sank into crisis along with other aspects of Nigerian life in 1993 when a presidential poll to restore democracy was annulled by his military predecessor.

But while Nigeria has achieved exchange rate stability and cut inflation to less than 30 percent from nearly 80 percent last December, gross domestic product growth has been inadequate at three percent to rub off Nigeria's 100 million people.
Inienger said the PRC was deeply concerned about the hardships faced by Nigerians and would announce definite measures to help alleviate them.
"The budget will touch the man on the street, the common man, that is why I said all Nigerians will smile," he said.

With Nigeria having reaped bountifully from a boom in crude oil prices in 1996 that looks likely to continue, the budget may allocate huge sums of money for restoring public infrastructure for the benefit of ordinary people as well as announce tax breaks.
Privatisation of state enterprises has also been on the cards to spur growth and induce physical development.
The challenge for the military government is coming up with a budget which stimulates growth without reviving inflation.

To ensure sustained development, Abacha recently set up a Vision 2010 committee headed by industrialist Ernest Shonekan to plan how to make Nigeria a developed economy by 2010, the 50th anniversary of the country's independence.
Shonekan's committee was scheduled to begin a four-day workshop in Abuja on Wednesday to consider how countries like Malaysia achieved their own economic miracles.
While the economic front is looking better, violence has increased with three bomb blasts in the country since December in which at least three soldiers have died and dozens were wounded.
The police blame the exiled wing of the opposition NADECO group for the violence. NADECO denies having had any role.
